section_summary: This section (pages 124–203) documents Allied and U.S. State Department efforts in August–October 1945 to locate, secure, and exploit Japanese government records, diplomatic archives, and military-technical intelligence following the surrender of Japan. It opens with extensive USFET G-2 intelligence reports and an in-depth study of captured Japanese correspondence from Berlin detailing German-Japanese technical cooperation in aviation, armaments, and machine tools, as well as the collapsing morale and living conditions of Japanese personnel in Germany. The remainder of the section focuses on worldwide diplomatic maneuvers across neutral and Allied capitals—including Bogota, Havana, Ciudad Trujillo, Ottawa, Vatican City, Beirut, Brussels, Mexico City, Ankara, and Bangkok—to prevent the destruction of Japanese diplomatic archives and negotiate custody among the Four Powers, which remained complicated by delays in directives from General MacArthur's headquarters in Tokyo.

subfiles.about: Catalogues captured papers of the Japanese Naval Attaché in Berlin concerning European war production, naval construction, finance, and intelligence.
subfiles.from: Office of Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Headquarters, U.S. Forces, European Theater (Main) (Lt. Col. Dupre Sassard)
subfiles.summary: This report indexes captured documents from the Japanese Embassy in Berlin dating from 1943 to 1945, recovered by the Japanese Intelligence Section of USFET. The materials include records on European resources and the international situation in 1943, naval construction, anti-aircraft defense, expenses of the Finance Attaché, and diplomatic telegrams. The original documents were forwarded to MIRS in Washington via London.
subfiles.title: Japanese Document Report: Papers of the Japanese Naval Attache, Berlin

subfiles.about: Reports on captured blueprints for German industrial machinery and hydrogenation plants destined for Japan.
subfiles.from: Office of Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Headquarters, U.S. Forces, European Theater (Main) (Lt. Col. Dupre Sassard)
subfiles.summary: Documents captured at the Japanese Embassy in Berlin in July 1945 by the Japanese Intelligence Section, USFET, are catalogued for transmission to Washington. The collection contains blueprints for various motors, blueprints from I.G. Farben headquarters for a hydrogenation plant, and miscellaneous technical blueprints. Distribution was made to various Allied military, naval, and air intelligence authorities.
subfiles.title: Japanese Document Report CD-137: Blue Prints for Machinery for Japan

subfiles.about: Details the agreement Aktion 'I.A.' between Germany and Japan returning purchased German armaments and aircraft for European combat use.
subfiles.from: Office of Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Headquarters, U.S. Forces, European Theater (Main) (Lt. Col. Dupre Sassard)
subfiles.summary: The report catalogues six folders of correspondence regarding an agreement dated September 15, 1944 (code-named Aktion 'I.A.') between the Reichswirtschaftsministerium and Japanese military and naval attaches in Berlin. Under this agreement, German armaments and machine tools purchased by Japan but awaiting shipment in Germany were temporarily released to strengthen German armed forces. Equipment included sample German aircraft (Me 109, Me 210, Do 217, Ju 88, Fw 190, DFS 230), Tiger and Panther tanks, anti-tank Pak equipment, 88mm and 105mm Flak guns, and aircraft cannons.
subfiles.title: Japanese Document Report CD-138: Return of German Armaments bought by Japanese to Germany

subfiles.about: Summarizes captured records documenting Japanese negotiations with German manufacturers for aircraft engines and optical equipment.
subfiles.from: Office of Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Headquarters, U.S. Forces, European Theater (Main) (Lt. Col. Dupre Sassard)
subfiles.summary: Documents captured in Berlin by USSTAF detail Japanese efforts from 1939 to 1945 to purchase Argus aircraft engines (notably As 410) and obtain reproduction rights through Ernst Prieger. It also records the May 1941 visit of the Sakaraki Commission to the C.P. Goerz plant in Berlin-Zehlendorf. Additional files found at the Zeiss-Ikon plant in Berlin-Steglitz reflect Japanese procurement of Goerz optical and reconnaissance equipment.
subfiles.title: Japanese Document Report CD-139: Japanese Contacts with German Manufacturers of Air Equipment

subfiles.about: Lists sixteen categories of captured Japanese naval technical documents concerning aircraft, armaments, machine tools, and navigation gear.
subfiles.from: Office of Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Headquarters, U.S. Forces, European Theater (Main) (Lt. Col. Dupre Sassard)
subfiles.summary: Documents seized in July 1945 from the Japanese Naval Attaché in Berlin encompass technical plans and correspondence with prominent European manufacturers. Subject matter includes machine tools by Niles-Werke, Loewe, and others; aircraft radio and blind landing systems; automatic cannons from Oerlikon, Hispano-Suiza, and Rheinmetall-Borsig; aircraft engines from BMW, Argus, and Heinkel; Tavaro fuses; Goerz navigational aids; Hagenuk smoke apparatus; and analyses of Allied equipment such as the Sperry bombsight.
subfiles.title: Japanese Document Report CD-140: Aircraft & Equipment - Correspondence with Japanese

subfiles.about: Catalogues forty files of technical reports, purchase records, and intelligence data on German and Japanese aviation spanning 1936 to 1942.
subfiles.from: Office of Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Headquarters, U.S. Forces, European Theater (Main) (Lt. Col. Dupre Sassard)
subfiles.summary: This inventory covers correspondence, blueprints, and intelligence reports found in the Japanese Naval Attaché's office in Berlin. Contents include German aircraft production studies, Heinkel manufacturing data, notes on Allied aircraft performances, purchase records for naval supplies, lists of Japanese students and nationals in Berlin (1941-1942), and correspondence regarding Swiss precision instruments. The records reflect extensive Japanese technical intelligence gathering on German and foreign aeronautical technology.
subfiles.title: Japanese Document Report CD/141: Japanese & German Aircraft - Reports and Correspondence

subfiles.about: Inventories Japanese Naval Air Attaché records showing widespread negotiations to purchase machine tools from German and Swiss manufacturers.
subfiles.from: Office of Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Headquarters, U.S. Forces, European Theater (Main) (Lt. Col. Dupre Sassard)
subfiles.summary: Documents recovered from the Japanese Embassy in Berlin in August 1945 consist of specifications, drawings, and correspondence dating from 1941 to 1943. They document Japanese negotiations to procure presses, lathes, milling machines, and grinding equipment from dozens of specialized firms across Germany and Switzerland, including Deutsche Niles-Werke, Wanderer-Werke, Schloemann, Carl Zeiss, and Askania-Werke. The materials were prepared for transmission to Washington via London.
subfiles.title: Japanese Document Report CD-142: Japanese Interest in German Machine Tools

subfiles.about: Details thirty-four captured folders concerning Japanese procurement of German aircraft engines, weapons, electronics, and technical licenses.
subfiles.from: Office of Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Headquarters, U.S. Forces, European Theater (Main) (Lt. Col. Dupre Sassard)
subfiles.summary: This report indexes records from the Japanese Naval (Air) Attaché's office in Berlin covering 1940 through 1943. Key files document contracts for Argus, Daimler-Benz, BMW, and Jumo aircraft engines; VDM and Schwarz propellers; Oerlikon and Mauser aircraft cannons; Bosch electrical equipment; and aerial photography systems from Zeiss. The collection also includes intelligence files on Allied air forces and technical evaluations of the Fw 200 Condor and German torpedoes.
subfiles.title: Japanese Document Report CD/143: Japanese Interest in German Air Equipment

subfiles.about: Summarizes documents and photographs concerning General Tani's mission to the Eastern Front to observe German railway bridge engineering.
subfiles.from: Office of Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Headquarters, U.S. Forces, European Theater (Main) (Lt. Col. Dupre Sassard)
subfiles.summary: Materials captured at Berlin-Tempelhof on August 8, 1945, describe General Tani's official mission from Berlin to the Moscow front. The files include detailed engineering reports, maps, and photographs of German railway bridge reconstruction on the Russian front between June 23 and July 8, 1944. Also included are a December 1938 study on French aircraft and private photographs of General Tani.
subfiles.title: Japanese Document Report CD/144: Japanese Study of German Bridge Reconstruction

subfiles.about: Provides a detailed inventory of technical files from the Japanese Naval-Air Attaché covering German military aircraft, engines, instruments, and armaments.
subfiles.from: Office of Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Headquarters, U.S. Forces, European Theater (Main) (Lt. Col. Dupre Sassard)
subfiles.summary: This report catalogues voluminous technical documentation spanning 1939 to 1945 recovered from the Japanese Embassy in Berlin. The records encompass operational manuals, plans, and specifications for dozens of German combat aircraft (Messerschmitt, Focke-Wulf, Junkers, Dornier, Heinkel) and engines (Daimler-Benz, BMW, Jumo, Argus). Further sections list Askania and Contraves measuring instruments, Lorenz and Telefunken radio equipment, bombsights, aircraft armament, and American, British, and Russian orders of battle.
subfiles.title: Japanese Document Report CD/145: Documents taken from the Japanese Naval-Air Attache's Office in the Japanese Embassy, Berlin

subfiles.about: Instructs diplomatic missions to prevent the destruction of Japanese archives pending confirmation of Emperor Hirohito's surrender directives.
subfiles.summary: Secretary Byrnes informs missions that the War Department has requested General MacArthur to have the Japanese Emperor issue instructions to Japanese overseas missions and protecting powers regarding the surrender of property and archives. Pending confirmation that these instructions have been issued, American representatives are directed to make every effort to prevent the destruction of Japanese archives worldwide.
subfiles.title: Circular Telegram to American Diplomatic Missions on Preserving Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Reports the Spanish Chargé d'Affaires' intention to transfer intact Japanese archives in Cuba to the Cuban Government.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Norweb reports that Spanish Chargé d'Affaires García Olay proposed to turn Japanese archives over to the Cuban Government under standing instructions, despite not receiving fresh word from Madrid. The Cuban Ministry of State confirmed the transfer was imminent. The Spanish Chargé stated that the archives remained completely intact inside wirebound boxes with unbroken seals.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 570 from Habana regarding Japanese Archives in Cuba

subfiles.about: Informs that Colombian plainclothes police surveillance has been placed inside the Japanese Legation in Bogota.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Wiley reports advice from the Colombian Foreign Office that plainclothes surveillance has been instituted inside the Japanese Legation pending the return of the Swiss Chargé d'Affaires. This security measure follows earlier warnings regarding the vulnerability of Japanese records.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1141 from Bogota on Surveillance of Japanese Legation

subfiles.about: Reports efforts to secure Japanese archives in Bogota and detain a gardener believed to hold key documents, amid Soviet interest.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Wiley relates difficulties in contacting the absent Swiss Chargé d'Affaires while the Swiss Legation remains unable to act without instructions. Prompted by a Swiss clerk's warning that the Japanese gardener possessed the most sensitive records, Wiley urged the Colombian Foreign Minister to detain the gardener and his family. The Foreign Minister also noted that the Soviet Minister had sought an appointment, apparently determined to prevent the archives from entering American hands.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1139 from Bogota regarding Japanese Archives and Caretaker

subfiles.about: Advises that preliminary inspection shows voluminous Japanese archives in Bogota are written almost entirely in Japanese.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Wiley sends a brief preliminary report based on information from the Legal Attaché. The recovered Japanese archives are described as voluminous and composed almost exclusively in the Japanese language, with a complete report promised the following day.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1149 from Bogota on Preliminary Examination of Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Discusses British instructions for joint Allied custody of Japanese archives in Colombia and arrangements to transfer them to the Swiss Legation.
subfiles.summary: The British Ambassador in Bogota received instructions to seek joint British, American, and Soviet custody of Japanese archives upon formal surrender, though he favored transferring them to Wiley or sending them to Washington for processing. The Swiss Chargé d'Affaires telephoned approval to move the official archives from the Japanese Legation to the Swiss Legation, which the Legal Attaché's staff carried out using a truck. Efforts were also made to secure documents held by the Japanese gardener.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1146 from Bogota on Four-Power Custody and Transfer of Archives

subfiles.about: Reports Madrid's authorization for the Spanish Embassy to surrender Japanese archives and property to the Cuban Government.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Norweb reports that the Spanish Chargé d'Affaires received definitive instructions from Madrid to notify the Cuban Foreign Office of Spain's willingness to surrender all Japanese archives and property. The Spanish note cites the severance of Spanish-Japanese diplomatic relations on April 15. The formal transfer was scheduled to occur the following day.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 573 from Habana on Spanish Surrender of Japanese Property

subfiles.about: Transmits an Ottawa Embassy memorandum of conversation regarding Japanese property and archives in Canada.
subfiles.summary: A brief internal State Department routing slip from the Special War Problems Division (SWP) forwards an attached memorandum of conversation from Ottawa concerning Japanese property in Canada to Oscar S. Straus in the Foreign Activity Correlation Division.
subfiles.title: Routing Slip Transmitting Ottawa Memorandum on Japanese Property in Canada

subfiles.about: Records discussions with Canadian External Affairs regarding protecting powers and custody of Japanese archives in Canada.
subfiles.summary: Robert English reports on an informal conversation with Max Wershoff of the Canadian Department of External Affairs regarding Japanese archives. Wershoff explained that after Spain asked to be relieved of protecting Japanese interests, Switzerland was approached but never assumed actual duties, leaving the Spanish Consul General still acting and willing to surrender files. The Canadian Government chose to await formal legal steps before taking custody, believing the archives contained little of value.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on Japanese Archives in Canada

subfiles.about: Reports the search of the Japanese Legation in Bogota, transfer of key files to the Swiss, and discovery of five locked safes.
subfiles.summary: Legal Attaché personnel, accompanied by Swiss officials, completed a thorough search of the Japanese Legation premises and moved two cabinet loads of files and films to the Swiss Legation. Approximately two truckloads of commercial and propaganda literature remain sealed on site. Five locked combination safes remain in the sealed section, with the Japanese gardener claiming no knowledge of their contents or combinations.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1153 from Bogota on Search of Japanese Legation and Safes

subfiles.about: Reports the inspection and transfer of Japanese honorary consulate archives in Ciudad Trujillo to the Dominican Foreign Office.
subfiles.from: American Embassy, Ciudad Trujillo (J. F. McGurk)
subfiles.summary: Ambassador McGurk reports that Spanish Minister Schwartz delivered a package of archives formerly held by Manuel Menéndez, former Japanese Honorary Consul in Ciudad Trujillo. The package was opened on August 31 before representatives of the United States, Britain, China, and the Dominican Republic, revealing consular operational files, flags, and a wooden shield. Records showed Menéndez was appointed in 1939 and resigned in August 1941, having reported on wartime neutrality and political cartoons; finding no intelligence of permanent value, the Allies agreed to transfer the material to the Dominican Foreign Office.
subfiles.title: Despatch No. 306: Japanese Government Archives in Ciudad Trujillo

subfiles.about: Analyzes private letters and reports of captured Japanese officials in Germany, assessing their deteriorating morale, wartime hardships, and ideology.
subfiles.summary: This extensive three-part intelligence report examines twenty-six files of correspondence comprising sixty letters written between 1941 and 1945 by twenty-eight Japanese officials, military attaches, and technicians in wartime Germany. Part I presents a topical analysis covering air raid devastation, severe food and consumer shortages, relations with their German hosts, and capital flight remittances to hedge against inflation. Part II provides classified quotations categorized into defeatist sentiments and stubborn determination ('gambari'), illustrating anxiety over Allied advances in the Pacific and in Europe. Part III concludes that by late 1944 most Japanese residents in Germany were gripped by hysteria and privately convinced the war was lost.
subfiles.title: Report on the Examination of Correspondence Taken from Japanese Official Personnel Captured in Germany

subfiles.about: Distributes copies of Ciudad Trujillo Despatch No. 306 regarding Japanese archives to military and intelligence agencies.
subfiles.from: Department of State (FC: Oscar S. Straus)
subfiles.summary: The State Department transmits copies of Despatch No. 306 from Ciudad Trujillo dated September 4, 1945, to the Military Intelligence Division, Office of Naval Intelligence, FBI, and OSS for their information. The enclosure details the disposition of Japanese consular records in the Dominican Republic.
subfiles.title: Transmittal of Despatch No. 306 on Japanese Archives in Ciudad Trujillo
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division, Office of Naval Intelligence, Federal Bureau of Investigation, Office of Strategic Services

subfiles.about: Records British Embassy inquiries regarding Allied seizure of Japanese archives and the reported creation of an Allied Council for Japan.
subfiles.from: E. R. Dickover (Office of Far Eastern Affairs)
subfiles.summary: F. C. Everson of the British Embassy met with E. R. Dickover to seek information on Allied procedures for seizing Japanese diplomatic archives and property abroad, expressing surprise that the United States acted without prior consultation. Everson also queried press reports that General MacArthur had formed a four-power Allied Council to assist in governing Japan, commenting that such a step would be unexpected without consulting principal Allies.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on Allied Custody of Japanese Archives and Allied Council

subfiles.about: Inquires whether the Legation in Beirut approves having an OSS representative summarize seized Japanese archives.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary Acheson informs the Beirut Legation that the Office of Strategic Services (OSS) indicated its local representative is prepared to summarize the Japanese archives reported in Beirut's telegram 274. Acheson requests the Minister's views on the proposal.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 272 to Beirut on Summarizing Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Reports joint demarche to the Holy See to prevent destruction of Japanese Embassy archives in Vatican City.
subfiles.from: American Chargé at the Vatican (Harold H. Tittmann, Jr.)
subfiles.summary: Following consultation with his Chinese colleague and with the British Minister associating himself, Tittmann addressed a note to the Vatican on August 31 requesting that Japanese officials avoid destroying or removing Embassy archives pending instructions. Tittmann notes that most archives were probably destroyed long ago, anticipating only an unimportant residue, and inquires whether recovered documents should be processed by Rome area G-2.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 195 from Vatican City on Japanese Archives and Vatican Demarche

subfiles.about: Reports taking custody of Japanese archives and consular property in Beirut and requests instructions on inspection.
subfiles.summary: Minister Wadsworth took delivery on behalf of the Four Powers of Japanese archives and property from the Spanish Consulate gérant, who had held them since the Argentine Consulate General closed in 1943. Wadsworth secured concurrence from the Lebanese Premier, the departing British Minister, and the Soviet Minister. The Legation holds sixteen sealed wooden cases of archives and several packages of personal effects of the former Japanese Consul who departed in 1941, requesting guidance on joint Allied inspection.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 274 from Beirut on Surrender of Japanese Archives and Consular Effects

subfiles.about: Transmits Swedish Legation report that no surrender instructions have been received from Tokyo regarding Japanese property in Belgium.
subfiles.summary: The Swedish Legation in Brussels informed the American Embassy that it had received no word from the Japanese Government regarding the surrender of diplomatic and consular archives and property to Allied authorities. Sawyer requests that the Department arrange for the necessary surrender instructions to be transmitted to Tokyo.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1132 from Brussels on Japanese Property Instructions

subfiles.about: Discusses strategy for securing Japanese archives in Mexico through Mexican custody rather than asserting direct joint Allied possession.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Messersmith discusses tactical delays in claiming Japanese property pending the signing of surrender documents and MacArthur's directives to Tokyo. He describes conferences with his British, Chinese, and Soviet colleagues in Mexico City, recommending that the Four Powers ask the Mexican Government to seize the archives and share their contents, rather than insisting on joint Allied custody which would irritate Mexican sovereignty. Messersmith also notes unsubstantiated reports that outgoing Japanese diplomats hid sensitive documents with private Japanese residents in Mexico City.
subfiles.title: Letter from Ambassador Messersmith on Japanese Archives and Property in Mexico
subfiles.to: John W. Carrigan (Chief, Division of Mexican Affairs)

subfiles.about: Informs Embassy Panama that definitive instructions await Tokyo developments and approves local transfer of archives.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary Acheson advises Embassy Panama that because of the situation explained in the August 29 circular telegram, no conclusive instructions can be provided regarding Japanese archives. The Department approves the action reported in Panama's telegram 836 transferring seized archives into the Embassy Office Building.
subfiles.title: Telegram to Panama regarding Japanese Archives in Panama

subfiles.about: Confirms the transfer of remaining Japanese archives seized by Panamanian authorities into the American Embassy Office Building.
subfiles.summary: Chargé d'Affaires Donnelly reports that pursuant to an informal arrangement with the Panamanian Foreign Office, the few remaining Japanese archives that had been seized by the Panamanian Government were safely moved into the American Embassy Office Building on September 7.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 836 from Panama on Transfer of Seized Japanese Archives

subfiles.about: Reports a conversation with the Soviet Chargé d'Affaires in Mexico regarding Japanese archives, intervened property, and reparations.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Messersmith transmits a memorandum of his discussion with the Soviet Chargé d'Affaires, whom he informed that Allied action on Japanese archives was suspended awaiting instructions from Washington. They also discussed intervened German and Japanese assets in Mexico, with Messersmith explaining that under reparations policies Latin American republics must look to enemy property within their own territories for indemnification.
subfiles.title: Letter and Memorandum of Conversation on Soviet Discussions regarding Japanese Property in Mexico
subfiles.to: John Willard Carrigan (Chief, Division of Mexican Affairs)

subfiles.about: Records the withdrawal and charging out of document file 894.414/9-1145 in August 1960.
subfiles.summary: A standard State Department archival charge-out card (Form DS-1033) recording that file item 894.414/9-1145 was charged out from central records on August 18, 1960.
subfiles.title: Charge-Out Record for File 894.414/9-1145

subfiles.about: Reviews the history and complications of obtaining custody of Japanese overseas archives pending MacArthur's orders in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Frederick B. Lyon (FC) and Oscar S. Straus (FC)
subfiles.summary: Frederick B. Lyon and Oscar S. Straus outline the impasse confronting American diplomatic missions worldwide that demanded custody of Japanese archives following the August 14 circular. When the Swiss approached Tokyo, the Japanese Government replied that the Potsdam Declaration did not provide for surrendering overseas archives, and General MacArthur deferred issuing enforcement orders until propitious. The memorandum asks whether missions should await orders that may take months and whether Japan will be permitted future diplomatic representation abroad.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Dilemma Over Custody of Japanese Diplomatic Archives and Property

subfiles.about: Reports postponing a Soviet proposal for immediate tripartite takeover of Japanese archives in Colombia.
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Wiley reports attending a meeting called by the Soviet Minister, who proposed immediate joint tripartite action by the Soviet, British, and American missions to take custody of the Japanese archives in Bogota. Backed by the British Ambassador, Wiley succeeded in postponing any action until receiving further instructions from the Department, welcoming Washington's concurrence that he act as sole joint custodian.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1185 from Bogota on Soviet Pressure for Joint Action on Archives

subfiles.about: Discusses coordinating with the British and OSS to prevent the destruction of Japanese archives in Bangkok.
subfiles.from: Abbott Low Moffat (SEA) and Oscar S. Straus (FC)
subfiles.summary: Straus and Moffat discussed handling Japanese archives in Bangkok upon Thailand's severance of relations with Japan, with SEA sending advice via OSS channels that Thailand could permit transfer to a neutral protecting power such as Sweden or Switzerland. Because British forces control Bangkok, it was agreed that the OSS representative should contact the British locally to ensure steps are taken to prevent the destruction of Japanese archives.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation on Japanese Archives in Bangkok

subfiles.about: Urges the State Department to seize records of the Japanese Black Dragon Society to identify members in the United States.
subfiles.from: Representative Gerald W. Landis (House of Representatives)
subfiles.summary: Congressman Gerald W. Landis writes to Secretary Byrnes urging that occupation authorities seize the files of the ultranationalist Black Dragon Society in Japan. He emphasizes that these records would be highly valuable in locating and investigating society members operating within the United States.
subfiles.title: Letter from Representative Gerald W. Landis on Black Dragon Society Files

subfiles.about: Informs Congressman Landis that Black Dragon Society files were reportedly destroyed, but military search continues.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary Acheson responds to Congressman Landis's inquiry of September 13 concerning the records of the Black Dragon Society. Acheson explains that society members claimed their files were destroyed during springtime air raids or deliberately burned by members, and notes that while the Army is actively searching for significant files, no documents have yet been found.
subfiles.title: Letter to Representative Gerald W. Landis regarding Black Dragon Society Files
subfiles.to: Representative Gerald W. Landis (House of Representatives)

subfiles.about: Recommends keeping overseas Japanese archives in abeyance pending MacArthur's orders and examines future Japanese representation.
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine (Director, Office of Far Eastern Affairs - FE)
subfiles.summary: Ballantine responds to questions raised in FC's September 11 memorandum regarding overseas Japanese archives and property. He advises leaving the matter in abeyance pending orders from General MacArthur to the Japanese Government, suggesting a circular instructing missions to desist from further action in the interim. On the question of postwar Japanese diplomatic representation, he notes no United States policy decision has been reached, though the British favor eliminating Japanese missions abroad.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Diplomatic Representation and Overseas Japanese Archives
subfiles.to: Frederick B. Lyon (Chief, Division of Foreign Activity Correlation - CON)

subfiles.about: Informs Embassy Ankara that a definitive statement on Japanese archives is impossible and advises leaving custody with the Swiss.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary Acheson replies to Ankara's telegrams 1191 and 1218, stating that a definitive decision regarding Japanese archives is impossible at this time due to the evolving situation in Tokyo. In the interim, the Department believes that the Swiss Legation should retain custody of the archives.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 920 to Ankara on Custody of Japanese Archives in Turkey

subfiles.about: Records briefing George Atcheson, Jr., on the urgency of having MacArthur order the surrender of overseas Japanese archives.
subfiles.summary: Oscar S. Straus spoke with George Atcheson, Jr., who was departing immediately to serve as Political Adviser to General MacArthur in Tokyo. Straus emphasized that American missions abroad were left in an awkward position after demanding Japanese archives, and urged that MacArthur promptly direct the Japanese Government to order its overseas missions and protecting powers to surrender their archives. Atcheson promised to bring the urgent matter directly to MacArthur's attention.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation with George Atcheson, Jr., on Japanese Archives Problem

subfiles.about: Recommends assigning an OSS representative attached to the Legation to examine seized Japanese archives in Beirut.
subfiles.summary: Minister Wadsworth responds to the Department's telegram 272 regarding the Japanese archives held at the Legation in Beirut. He states that he sees no objection to authorizing a staff member to examine the materials, proposing to assign the OSS representative on his staff to perform the survey.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 286 from Beirut on Assigning OSS Representative to Examine Archives

subfiles.about: Authorizes the Beirut Legation to have an OSS representative examine Japanese archives and submit an intelligence report.
subfiles.summary: Acting Secretary Acheson authorizes Minister Wadsworth to have an OSS representative or other qualified staff member examine the Japanese archives held in Beirut. Acheson instructs that a comprehensive report with hectograph copies be submitted to the Department for the attention of the Chief of the Division of Foreign Activity Correlation for distribution to interested intelligence agencies.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 280 to Beirut Authorizing Examination of Japanese Archives
